prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at that angle, opening the field of moire quantum materials.

statement.case_for: After the full first round I keep B042 as a single achievement with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer. My reason is scientific and has not changed: the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model is a minimal, analytically transparent model that predicts a sharp and non-obvious condition (the magic angle at which the Dirac velocity vanishes and the lowest bands flatten) in a structure with a huge moire unit cell, and nature then showed correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle. The mechanism, band flattening by interlayer tunnelling and interference, is simple and general, which is why it transferred to other graphene multilayers and to transition-metal dichalcogenide moire systems and to a large independent literature. I want to be clear about what the prize would reward: the prediction and the experimental demonstration that a flat-band moire system hosts strongly correlated states. It would not reward a theory of the superconductivity. I do not move on configuration, but I move on emphasis: the weakness I conceded in round 1 (maturity of the interpretation) is, after reading Lindroth and Kroll, a more serious point than I first treated it, and I now regard B012 as a genuinely close second and not merely a courtesy alternative.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against my choice is the one Lindroth and Kroll press: the flat-band prediction and the existence of correlated states are firm, but the interpretation of those states, the nature of the insulators and the pairing mechanism, is not stable, and twist-angle disorder still limits sample-to-sample comparison. A prize about a young field risks looking early if the interpretation shifts. Credit is also messier than for B012. The three names must cover a theory pair and an experimental group; Yuan Cao as first author, Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto for the earlier continuum description, and the Dean, Young, Yacoby, Efetov and Yazdani groups all stand outside the three. B012 has two names whose roles (concept and first realisation, record accuracy and many-body clock work) are distinct and agreed by all who rank it, and its quantitative claims are cross-checked by several independent laboratories at the 1e-18 level. If the committee regards settled maturity and clean attribution as decisive, B012 is the better prize.

responses.point: Lindroth separates the solid flat-band prediction and its confirmation from the unstable interpretation of the correlated states, and holds the latter against recognition now; she also says the attribution problem is larger for B042 than for the lattice clock.
responses.response: I accept the separation and I think it is the right way to frame the dispute, but I draw a different conclusion from it. What I would reward is exactly the first half, a prediction made with a transparent model and a measured consequence at the predicted angle; the citation should say 'correlated insulating and superconducting states' as an observation, not as an explained phenomenon. That is the same logic as the cuprates, where the discovery was recognised long before the mechanism. Where I concede to you is attribution: it is cleaner for B012, and a three-name split with one experimental name is a real compromise, not a neat one. If you can tell me which of the two halves of the B042 story you would still accept as prize-worthy on its own, that would help me judge whether our disagreement is about maturity or only about credit.

responses.point: Kroll supports B012 because the lattice clock is a concrete, quantitative technique reproduced and compared at 1e-18 by JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and NPL, with the cleanest two-name credit on the shortlist, and he names the 2005 and 2012 prizes as the main objection.
responses.response: I take the quantitative evidence for B012 seriously and I do not doubt the physics. On the chair's question about the 2005 and 2012 prizes, my reading as a theorist is that the magic-wavelength condition is a distinct idea: it removes the light shift of the clock transition for a trapped neutral ensemble and thereby changes the statistics of the measurement, which neither the comb nor ion control did. I therefore do not think novelty is decisive against B012, and I would not want to use it as an argument for B042. My remaining difference with you is about what the prize recognises: B012 refines how precisely a known quantity can be measured, while B042 opens a new class of systems. I also want to note that the open questions you list, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Pal'chikov, are of the same kind as my Cao and Lopes dos Santos questions, so cleanliness of credit is a smaller gap between the two than it looks.

responses.point: Eriksson agrees with B042 on theory-then-experiment grounds, wants the citation worded around the prediction and the discovery rather than a person's role, and notes that the main discovery is no longer in doubt after eight years.
responses.response: I agree on the wording and have kept it: the citation names the prediction and the observation and says nothing about a mechanism or about who performed which measurement, so that it recognises the platform and not one group. I would add one caveat to your point that the discovery is no longer in doubt. The existence of the states is not in doubt, but the committee should not let that stand in for settled interpretation, and I would rather we say plainly in the public record that the pairing mechanism is open. We both list B030 as an alternative; on reflection I am less sure about it because of the 2016 overlap you mention and because the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe prediction makes the three-name allocation contested.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B042 first as a clean prediction followed by a decisive clue from nature, reproduced by many groups, and says he would not be embarrassed if the committee preferred the optical lattice clock.
responses.response: We agree on the sequence and I share your willingness to see B012 prevail. On the priority question you and I raised, I have looked again at how I would describe it. Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto (2007) derived a continuum description with an interlayer-coupling-induced Dirac-velocity reduction; Bistritzer and MacDonald (2011) gave the full calculation of the bands and located the flat-band magic angles, which is the result experiments tested. That supports crediting the 2011 work, but I cannot show it is airtight and I would not want to state it as established in a citation. I think the three of us who prefer B042 should say openly that this is where a critic of the prize would attack it, and that it is a reason the choice of B012 would be defensible.

uncertainties: Whether the 2007 continuum-model work of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto weakens the priority of Bistritzer and MacDonald enough to change the theory credit; my reading is that the 2011 magic-angle result is distinct, but I cannot call it settled.

Whether a committee can reward the prediction and the observation of correlated states while leaving the pairing mechanism open, or whether the open interpretation makes the prize premature at about eight years.
How to treat Yuan Cao and the other experimental groups within the three-name limit, and whether one experimental name next to two theory names is the best allocation.
How the committee should weigh B012's cleaner credit and maturity against B042's novelty as a new class of systems; I have not found a criterion that settles this without reference to prize history.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my earlier disclosure. I have no collaboration with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, or with any credited name on B012 or B030. I am in the Gothenburg physics environment close to Chalmers colleagues, but I know of no collaboration relevant to these candidates, and I see no reason to recuse myself on any shortlisted ballot.
